Summary 51

We analyze whole-genome sequencing data from 141,431 Chinese women generated for 52

non-invasive pregnancy testing (NIPT). We use these data to characterize the population 53

genetic structure of China, and to investigate genetic associations with maternal and 54

infectious traits. We show that the present day distribution of alleles is a function of both 55

ancient migration and very recent population movements. We reveal novel phenotype- 56

genotype associations, including several replicated associations with height and BMI, an 57

association between maternal age and a variant near EMB, and between twin pregnancy 58

and NRG1. Finally, we identify a unique pattern of circulating viral DNA in plasma with 59

high prevalence of hepatitis B and other clinically relevant maternal infections. A GWAS 60

for viral infections identifies an exceptionally strong association between integrated 61

herpesvirus 6 and MOV10L1, which affects piRNA processing and PIWI protein 62

function. These findings demonstrate the great value and potential of accumulating NIPT 63

data for worldwide medical and population genetic analyses. 64

Introduction 67

Sufficient large sample size is of fundamental importance in resolving biological 68

questions in population and medical genetics. Given a fixed budget, sample size tends to 69

play a more essential role compared to sequencing depth (Li et al., 2011). Previous 70

studies have demonstrated that sequencing many individuals at a low depth generally 71

provides a better representation of population genetic variation compared to sequencing a 72

more limited number of individuals at a higher depth (Fumagalli, 2013). Furthermore, 73

when using proper imputation techniques, even sequencing at an average depth of < 0.1x 74

in a large enough cohort can be a cost-effective strategy for detecting genetic associations 75

for complex traits (Pasaniuc et al., 2012). 76

Several large-scale national and international sequencing projects have been 77

carried out in the past decade with sample sizes limited to tens of thousands (Auton et al., 78

2015; Francioli et al., 2014; Gudbjartsson et al., 2015; Maretty et al., 2017; Walter et al., 79

2015). Increasing the sample sizes of these studies is a major financial and logistical 80

challenge. However, Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) for fetal trisomy - by 81

sequencing of maternal plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) (Zhang et al., 2015a) - has 82

become the fastest adopted molecular test in history and provide an untapped resource for 83

understanding population genetic variation and  genetic associations.  To date, over ten 84

millions of NIPT tests have been carried out globally, among which 70% were conducted 85

on Chinese women. These samples can be leveraged for population genetic investigations 86

of population history, large-scale genetic association studies, and viral screening if the 87

technical issues regarding the use of very large, very low depth (0.06x - 0.1x) samples 88

can be addressed. 89

Here, we analyze NIPT sequencing data of 141,431 pregnant women with 90

informed consent.  We demonstrate that allele frequencies can be estimated with high 91

accuracy, allowing further population genetic analyses.  We also show that efficient 92

genotype imputation is feasible and can provide considerable mapping power. We use the 93

data to carry out the hitherto largest analysis of population genetic variation in the 94

Chinese population, perform a genome-wide association study (GWAS) on multiple traits 95

in pregnant Chinese women, and survey the distribution of circulating viral DNA in the 96

maternal plasma. 97

Results 99

Study participants and chromosomal coverage 100

The 141,431 participants were recruited from 31 out of the 34 administrative divisions in 101

China (Figure S1A). Each individual was sequenced using 5-10 million single-end reads 102

(35-49bp), corresponding to a sequencing depth of 0.06x to 0.1x per individual (Figure 103

S1B). The reads were aligned to the hg19 reference using bwa10 (see STAR Methods), 104

with a resulting combined read depth distribution that is approximately Poisson and 105

closely follows that expected from the ENCODE mappability track (Figures S1C and 106

S1D). Based on read length and observed depth distribution we identified regions of the 107

genome accessible to high-confidence mapping in the NIPT data, resulting in a total 108

length of around 2.13 billion base pair accessible genome (75% of the non-N human 109


<!-- Page 7 -->


7

reference genome sequence). We also re-sequenced DNA derived from white blood cells 110

of 40 participants to a mean depth of 15x. These data were used in the variant calling and 111

genotype imputation evaluation. 112

Amount of genetic variations and accuracy of genotype imputation 113

Previous standard methods for allele frequency estimation and joint SNP calling, such as 114

those implemented in GATK (DePristo et al., 2011) and Samtools (Li, 2011) did not scale 115

up to sample sizes over a hundred thousand. Therefore, we developed a new method for 116

fast maximum likelihood estimation of allele frequencies and joint SNP calling using a 117

likelihood ratio test (STAR Methods). Using this method for initial screening, we 118

identified 32.5 million bi-allelic candidate SNPs (Table S1).  After recalibration using a 119

gaussian mixture model, we identified a final call set of 9.04 million single nucleotide 120

variants with a Transition/Transversion ratio of 2.1 for known variants and 2.4 for novel 121

variants, respectively (Figure S2A), consistent with those obtained for 1000 Genomes 122

Project (1KG) variants (Auton et al., 2015). 81.7% of the variants were called in the 1KG 123

Han Chinese individuals (Auton et al., 2015), ~16% of the variants were in the remainder 124

of 1KG or dbSNP database while 233,966 (2.6%) were novel variants (Figure 1A).  90% 125

of the variants were found in the union of the gnomAD East Asian (Lek et al., 2016) and 126

1KG Han Chinese call sets (Figure 1B).  Using experimental validation, we estimated an 127

upper bound for the false positive rate (FPR) of SNP calling of 0.2% (Figure S2B-E). 128

However, among novel variants the FPR was approx. 0.32.  These SNPs comprised a 129

small proportion of the total number of SNPs, but did include common variants, likely 130

due to unresolved mapping issues.  The squared correlation coefficient (R2) of the 131

frequency of the non-reference allele, i.e. alternative allele estimated in our study and that 132

computed in the 1KG Han Chinese was 0.98 (Figure 1C). 133

We subsequently imputed genotypes of 8.9 million known variable DNA sites 134

with allele frequency greater than 0.01 using the 1KG Han Chinese as a reference panel 135

(Flint et al., 2016) (STAR Methods). To estimate imputation accuracy, we compared the 136

squared correlation coefficient (R2) between the genotypes called in the medium coverage 137

whole genome sequencing data of the 40 individuals (MC set, 15x) and the imputed 138

genotypes in the low-coverage data (LC set).  2.13 million of the variants were well 139

imputed with an info score greater than 0.4, and with a p-value from a chi-square test of 140

Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium larger than 10-6. The mean imputation accuracy of those 141

variants was 0.89 while it was 0.71 for all variants combined (Figure 1D). The imputation 142

accuracy was negatively correlated to the fraction of fetal DNA present in the plasma but 143

the effect was not very pronounced (Figure S2F). 144

Population structure, recent population history and genetic adaptations 145

Even though the Chinese is the world’s largest population that comprises 1.4 billion 146

people, it is perhaps surprisingly understudied with respect to population genetic history. 147

We applied information of the 141, 431 pregnant women regarding digital geographic 148

location and self-reported ethnicity to study of the genetic variation in China at multiple 149

time scales. Because of the uncertainty in genotype calling, we conduct all population 150

genetic analyses using methods that either sample a single read per individual or use 151

maximum likelihood estimates of allele frequencies without relying on genotype 152

imputation. 153

A principal component analysis of all the 141, 431 participants suggested that the 154

first three principal components reflected sequencing read length, latitudinal genetic 155

differentiation and the sequencing error rate (Figure S3A-D). After removing participants 156

with 49bp read length and with sequencing error rate greater than 0.00325, a principal 157

component analysis of 45,387 self-reported Han Chinese from the 31 administrative 158

divisions showed that the greatest differentiation of Han Chinese is along a latitudinal 159

gradient (Figure SE-F), consistent with previous studies (Chen et al., 2009; Xu et al., 160

2009). In contrast, there is, perhaps surprisingly, very little differentiation from East to 161

West. This observation may be explained by the fact that a large proportion of the 162

western Han populations in China are recent immigrants organized by the central 163

government starting from 1949 when the People’s Republic of China was founded (Liang 164

and White, 1996). While the Han Chinese were found to be relatively genetically 165

homogenous, there was greater divergence among the minority ethnic groups for both 166

latitude and longitude (Figure 2A-B).  The most differentiated ethnic groups are the 167

Turkic speaking Uyghur and Kazakhs, who reside in the Xinjiang province, and the 168

Mongols residing primarily in Inner Mongolia. The Xibe, Tibetans, and Hui from central 169

China, the Yi from southwestern China, and the Zhuang and Buyi minorities from 170

southern China, also differ substantially from the Han Chinese that come from the same 171

area. On the other hand, the Manchu from northeastern China were genetically closest to 172

the Han Chinese in that area, consistent with historical accounts (Rhoads, 2000). 173

We further explored the patterns of allele sharing between Han Chinese and major 174

global ethnic groups using private alleles defined from the 1KG populations and using 175

outgroup F3 statistics (Peter, 2016) (STAR Methods). In the northwest and central west, 176

we observed private allele sharing with the 1KG European CEU panel both for 177

individuals self-identified as Han Chinese and for individuals self-identified as belonging 178

to a minority group. The strongest level of private allele sharing with the CEU was 179

observed for people in the most northwest provinces of Xinjiang and Gansu (Figure 2C), 180

likely reflecting the Turkic speaking ancestry in these minorities. When only the Han 181

Chinese were included, the strongest level of allele sharing with Europeans was observed 182

for people in the Qinghai, Gansu and Ningxia provinces (Figure 2D). These provinces are 183

located in the Hexi corridor, the most important commercial hub on the Silk Road 184

connecting China to the west since the establishment of the Han Dynasty (206 B.C.) 185

(Yang et al., 2008). Thus, one potential explanation for the Western ancestry observed in 186

these provinces is gene flow related to their location on the Silk Road. We also observed 187

a pattern of increased allele sharing with the 1KG Indian ITU reference panels in 188

southwestern populations from Xinjiang, Tibet, Yunnan, Guangxi and Hainan provinces 189

(Figure 2E-F), consistent with their geographic proximity to the Indian 190

subcontinent(Yang et al., 2017). Analyses based on the F3 statistic are mostly consistent 191

for the CEU analysis, but for the ITU analysis, we also show high affinity between the 192

Han Chinese in northern provinces and the ITU, likely due to the shared ancestry of the 193

CEU and ITU populations.    Furthermore, we applied the F3 statistic to learn patterns of 194

allele sharing between the Chinese provincial populations and 1KGP neighbour 195

populations including three Chinese populations, the Japanese and Vietnamese. We 196

observe a pattern of allele sharing among the thirty-three administrative divisions 197

reflecting the geographical origin of the 1KGP populations (Figure S3G-K). Interestingly, 198

we found that the CHB, although annotated as the Han Chinese from Beijing, did not 199

have the closest affinity with Beijing individuals but tended to be closer to populations in 200

This likely reflects the recent multiethnic migration into Beijing consistent with the 202

The difference in f3 statistic among provinces is very small, but all southern provinces 205

show more genetic affinity with other southern coastal provinces, while northern 206

provinces associate with northern coastal provinces(Results not shown). This observation 207

likely reflects a combination of internal migration events organized by the central 208

government since 1949 (Liang and White, 1996) and the country’s oriented movement of 209

labour from the interior to the coastal areas since 1979 (Liang and Ma, 2004). 210

We inferred selection within Han Chinese populations using two approaches. 211

First, we identified variants with significant differentiation along each PC compared to a 212

null distribution expected under a model of genetic drift (STAR Methods). Second, we 213

conducted a scan of the rarer but more important pathogenic variants in the Clinvar 214

database (Landrum et al., 2014) by statistically comparing allele frequency differences of 215

those loci among North, Central and South Han Chinese against a null distribution 216

generated from the genome-wide data. In the PC scan, we identified six loci showing 217

genome-wide significance across latitude: LILRA3, CR1, FADS2, DOCK9, ABCC11, and 218

a cluster of IGH genes (Figure 3A). The CR1, DOCK9, and the IGH genes display a 219

higher allele frequency in the south while the FADS2, ABCC11 and LILRA3 genes 220

display a higher derived allele frequency in the north (Figure 3B-G, Table S1).  Three of 221

these loci are known to be related to immune responses (the IGH genes, LILRA3 and 222

CR1).  DOCK9 is associated with bipolar disease and has been previously shown to under 223

selection in East Asians (Suo et al., 2012). FADS2 is a well-known target of selection 224

associated with changes in diet to, or from, a diet with a high content of animal fat, and 225

has previously been inferred to have been targeted by selection in Inuit (Fumagalli et al., 226

2015), South Asians (Kothapalli et al., 2016), Europeans (Buckley et al., 2017), and in 227

Africa (Mathias et al., 2012).  Our results suggest more recent selection has also been 228

acting within China. The ABCC11 locus is famously associated with earwax type and has 229

previously been shown to be under selection in Asian, Native American, and European 230

populations (Ohashi et al., 2011), and our results demonstrate that this locus is also under 231

differential selection within China. We also investigated the geographical distribution of 232

possibly pathogenic variants compiled from the ClinVar dataset (Landrum et al., 2014) as 233

candidates for loci under selection.  We calculated measures of allele frequency 234

differentiation (Fisher’s exact test between northern, central and southern Han Chinese, 235

comparing against a frequency-matched dataset of 100,000 SNPs chosen at random) 236

(STAR Methods).  We identified and reported the nine out of the 42,058 possibly 237

pathogenic variants in eight genes that display the most significant allele frequency 238

difference among the three geographical regions (Fisher exact test with p-value < 10-6, 239

percentile p-value < 5e-3, Figure 3H-O, Table S2). Those SNPs include rs72554665, a 240

polymorphic site in G6PD, a gene associated with resistance to malaria (Nkhoma et al., 241

Phenotype-genotype associations of multiple complex traits 244

In the following, we demonstrate that NIPT data can be used effectively in GWAS. 245

We first investigated associations with two common traits, height and body mass index 246

(BMI) among 61.7K individuals with both phenotypes recorded (Figure S4A-B).  We 247

applied a score test (Skotte et al., 2012) to test the association between the traits and the 248

genotype probabilities for each of the previously mentioned approx. 2 million imputed 249

variants, incorporating covariates such as the first to fifth principal components (Figure 250

S3A), maternal age, gestational age of the fetus, fetus sex, etc (STAR Methods). The 251

genomic control factor lambda for height and BMI were 1.51 and 1.32 respectively(QQ- 252

plots in Figure S4C-D). Due to the high polygenicity of the traits we also evaluated 253

inflation of our test statistics using LD-score regression which did not show severe 254

inflation (intercept 1.03, s.e. 0.03 and 1.10, s.e.  0.02, attenuation ratio 0.05, s.e. 0.04 and 255

0.24, s.e. 0.05 for height and BMI respectively), suggesting that confounding factors, 256

such as population structure, were generally well controlled (Table S4). The estimated 257

SNP heritability obtained from the LD score regression for height and BMI are 0.48 and 258

0.10, respectively. A comparison of the LD score regression statistics between Giant, UK 259

Biobank and our study can be found in Table S4. We note that strong inflation was 260

observed if covariates were not applied in the test model (genomic control factor lambda 261

for height and BMI are 9.71 and 2.68). 262

In total, 48 and 13 loci reached genome-wide significance for association with height 263

and BMI, respectively, at the classical 5x10-8 genome-wide significance level (Figure 4A- 264

B, Table 1). Forty-one of the height loci were previously reported, although only thirty- 265

six of them have previously been found in Asian populations (MacArthur et al., 2017). 266

Seven height loci located in or around the genes UBQLN2, MIR325HG, MAST2, 267

STRBP/ZBTB26, C11orf24-LRP5, ARHGEF12 and LINC00261 have not been previously 268

reported (Table 2, Figure S5A-F). There was one new signal in the intronic region of 269

DNA2, a locus first identified in GIANT (Wood et al., 2014) and another independent 270

signal in the nearby gene MYPN was reported (conditional p-value = 4.8e-8).  Three 271

BMI-associated loci in the genes PLD5, TRPC6 and CBLN4 were also not previously 272

reported (Table 2, Figure S5H-J). We attempted to replicate the novel and known 273

associations for height and BMI in 32,000 genotyped Chinese participants from the China 274

Kadoorie Biobank (CKB) cohort (Chen et al., 2011) and in the results of the GIANT 275

consortia (Yengo et al, BioRxiv) and the UK Biobank (Ben Neale’s website, STAR 276

0.463; UK Biobank, slope 0.434), respectively(Figure S4E-J). When comparing the beta 282

direction and the p-value of the lead or proxy SNPs between the discovery and test sets, 283

in almost all cases the p-values and the effect sizes of the SNPs are similar(Table 2, Table 284

The height and BMI results provide a proof of concept for the use of NIPT data in 290

GWAS and suggest that NIPT data can be used to investigate fertility and pregnancy 291

related traits that otherwise would be prohibitively difficult to investigate in such large 292

samples.   To illustrate this, we investigated associations for two novel traits: (1) maternal 293

age, which is expected to correlate with female fertility broadly defined, but may also be 294

affected by several other factors, and (2) twin pregnancy. The maternal age distribution 295

follows a bimodal distribution in the NIPT participants (Figure S4K). Similarly to height 296

and BMI, we again do not observe any severe inflation when including covariates for 297

both  maternal age (lambda=1.29) and twin pregnancy (lambda=1.06) (QQ plot see 298

Figure S4L-M). Strong inflation was also observed for these two traits if covariates were 299

not applied in the test model for maternal age (lambda=1.88) and twin pregnancy 300

(lambda=1.36). We find one significant association peak for maternal age located 301

between the HCN1 and EMB loci (rs16828019, p = 1.38E-11, Figures 4, S5K). This 302

signal is located near a previously identified association peak for age at first birth, 303

originally reported to be in the HCN1 gene (Barban et al., 2016).  Our lead SNP is closer 304

in location to EMB gene which encodes embigin, a transmembrane glycoprotein that 305

is preferentially expressed in the early stages of embryogenesis and enhances integrin- 306

mediated cell-substratum adhesion in mice (Huang et al., 1993). It shows particularly 307

high expression during early post implantation embryogenesis and is therefore a strong 308

candidate gene for further studies of infertility in humans. In European countries, 309

maternal age is associated with education attainment, which is a proxy for intelligence 310

(Barban et al., 2016). We don’t have records for education attainment in our study. 311

Whether education has an impact on maternal age in the Chinese population requires 312

further investigation. 313

Out of 137,646 individuals with ultrasound scans, 476 had more than one fetus 314

(e.g., twins). The lead associated SNP for this trait was located in the gene NRG1 315

(rs12056727, p=5.93E-9, odds ratio=1.99, Figures 4, S5L) and is a very strong eQTL for 316

expression in the thyroid (effect size = 0.5, p-value 1.2e-19) in the GTEx database 317

(Carithers and Moore, 2015). The tested allele T increases the twinning probability and 318

the NRG1 expression in the thyroid.  Furthermore, the SNP is associated with 319

hyperthyroidism in the UK BioBank (Sudlow et al., 2015) (p=1.7e-7, odds ratio = 1.15). 320

Thyroid function has previously been associated with fertility. The NRG1 gene has 321

mostly been investigated for its effects on behavior (schizophrenia in humans and 322

response to stress and anxiety in rodents), but at least one study notes that matings 323

between knockouts in mice have smaller litter size (Britto et al., 2004). However, the 324

exact reason for this is unknown.  More interestingly, twin pregnancies tend to be 325

associated with lower levels of the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)  (Soldin, 2006), 326

consistent with the SNP association with hyperthyroidism, which generally involves 327

increased thyroid hormone levels and decreased TSH levels. 328

Circulating viral DNA in maternal plasma 330

Despite its importance for public health, few studies have been carried out on the 331

distribution of viral DNA in blood plasma (the virome) at the population level.  However, 332

the sequence technologies used in NIPT studies provide an untapped resource for 333

understanding viral epidemiology.  We investigated the plasma virome of 138, 882 334

participants by querying reads that do not align to the human genome against the NCBI 335

viral sequence database (Sayers et al., 2009) using BLAST (Altschul et al., 1990) (STAR 336

Methods). The plasma virome, cleaned for phages and low prevalence virus, is 337

represented in (Figure 5A), and all observed viruses, without removing phage and low 338

abundance participants, can be found in Figure S6A-B. We examined sequencing 339

coverage to individual viruses to determine potential misclassification or contamination, 340

where prevalent viruses with relatively even coverage support true virus identification 341

(Figure S7). Most viruses detected have even sequence coverage, while a few display 342

localized peaks. To understand if these peaks are related to human homology, we aligned 343

viral reference sequences to the human reference genome, hg19 and non-EBV decoys 344

(Table S6). We found that only the localized peak of HCV corresponds to a human 345

homologous sequence, yet these sequences are only found in a small number of our 346

subjects (N=3). The peaks in coverage may represent highly conserved areas of viruses, 347

misclassification of human sequences, uneven production of viral DNA, select viral 348

integration events or introduced viral DNA from vaccine, further investigation and 349

validation is required. 350

Interestingly, the blood virome in a recent study of Europeans (Moustafa et al., 2017) 351

appeared to have a different viral distribution compared to the pregnant Chinese women 352

participants analyzed in this study (Figure 5A). The use of differing sequencing 353

approaches is a challenge to direct comparisons, but our participants were significantly 354

enriched for hepatitis B virus (HBV) and Parvovirus B19 DNA and showed a lower 355

prevalence of human herpesvirus 7 (HHV-7) DNA compared to Europeans (Moustafa et 356

al., 2017). The prevalence of HBV DNA across Chinese populations estimated in our 357

study is approximately 2.5% (with high mean abundance 25.6), which is less than the 358

9.8% prevalence reported in a Chinese 2014 population survey of HBV antibodies (IgM 359

to HBV core antigen or surface antigen(HBsAg+)) (Yan et al., 2014). These differences 360

are likely due to varying estimates derived from circulating HBV DNA versus antibody 361

prevalence, the enrichment of our sample for relatively affluent younger women, and the 362

late adoption of the HBV vaccine in China (since 1992)(Yan et al., 2014). We detected 363

3,421 participants for HBV DNA, yet 1,911 participants self-reported some type of HBV 364

infection. As expected, we have the greatest sensitivity (78.7%) to detect reported active 365

HBV infection (HBsAg+). Of 1032 individuals reporting latent infection (HBsAg-), we 366

detected HBV DNA in 53 subjects, where the lower sensitivity (5.1%) is likely due to 367

low levels of circulating HBV DNA during latent infection (Figure S6C). Interestingly, 368

we detected HBV DNA in 2,959 individuals who did not report any HBV infection, 369

suggesting an additional and potentially clinically important use of NIPT where 370

circulating HBV DNA is associated with fetal transmission(Zou et al., 2012). 371

We detected many hits for human endogenous retrovirus K (HERV-K) 372

(prevalence ~2.1%, mean abundance 0.22) which was previously shown to be active, 373

capable of expression in humans, and associated with HIV infection (Zwolińska et al., 374

2013). All humans carry multiple copies of HERV-K in their genomes and the recovery 375

of non-aligning HERV-K in a subset of subjects may be the result of insertionally 376

polymorphic HERV-K (Wildschutte et al., 2016), or the result of co-option of HERV-K 377

sequences by other exogenous viruses. Herpesvirus 6A/B (HHV-6A/B), the third most 378

common viral group, has a prevalence of 0.8% (mean abundance 0.48). HHV-6A/B were 379

grouped together due to high co-occurrence and potential for misclassification due to 380

sequence homology. A distinct bimodal distribution clusters high abundance HHV-6A/B 381

(Abundance>10-0.5, Figure 5A), likely separating chromosomally integrated HHV-6A/B 382

(ciHHV-6A/B) from non-integrated circulating HHV-6A/B as noted in previous studies 383

(Moustafa et al., 2017).  Human herpesvirus 5 or cytomegalovirus (HHV-5 or CMV) is 384

the fourth most common infection with a prevalence of 0.40% (mean abundance 0.03). 385

This virus is of particular interest in pregnant women as CMV is one of the leading 386

causes of birth defects(Cheeran et al., 2009).   Parvovirus B19 has a prevalence of 0.39% 387

(mean abundance 1.68) and is of clinical relevance to pregnant women as active infection 388

can cause fetal anemia and death. 389

To identify germline polymorphisms associated with viral infections we carried 390

out an association study for each of the major viruses, comparing infected individuals to a 391

control group of 90,531 participants who have no detectable virus in the NIPT 392

sequencing data. We identified an intronic variant, rs73185306, in the MLC1-MOV10L1 393

region that is significantly associated with the presence of high abundance ciHHV-6A/B 394

(N=653) but not low abundance HHV-6A/B (N=1556)  (Odds ratio = 3.4, p-value = 7.3e- 395

66) (Figure 5B-C, Figure S6D).  rs73185306 is an expression quantitative trait locus 396

(eQTL) for both MCL1 and MOV10L1 genes suggesting a functional role (Lonsdale et al., 397

2013). To ensure that this strong association was not due to alignment error and 398

homology in the MLC1-MOV10L1 region, we aligned HHV-6A and HHV-6B genomes 399

back to the human genome and found no sequence homology in this genomic region 400

(Table S7). The MCL1 gene is involved in myeloid cell differentiation and has been 401

shown to be upregulated during herpesvirus infection (CMV, EBV and HHV-8). The 402

MOV10L1 gene is known to be associated with platelet distribution (Astle et al., 2016) 403

which is also correlated with severity of Hepatitis B infection (Karagoz et al., 2014), 404

though we found no association with circulating HBV DNA. Intriguingly, MOV10L1 is a 405

PIWI interacting RNA helicase that is active during spermatogenesis and functions as a 406

repressor of retrotransposons (Vourekas et al., 2015). We suspect that the PIWI- 407

interacting RNA represses HHV-6A/B integration and polymorphisms in this gene allow 408

for more efficient integration of HHV-6A/B during spermatogenesis. We observed no 409

other significant genome wide SNP associations with other viruses. 410

Finally, we explored the geographic distribution of detected viruses in the studied 411

population throughout China.  We mapped the prevalence of viral sequences among 30 412

administrative divisions with more than 100 participants. Tibet was excluded due to a 413

small sample size of 13 individuals. We observed different geographic patterns for many 414

viruses (Figure 5D-F, Figure S6E-J). We observed that HBV DNA in serum has a higher 415


<!-- Page 21 -->


21

prevalence in southern China compared to central and northern China (Figure 5D), while 416

previous studies have shown higher HBV antibody prevalence in northern China (Yan et 417

al., 2014). We speculate that subgenotype resolution differences in HBV may contribute 418

to circulating DNA levels, a clinically relevant predictor of fetal HBV transmission and 419

tumor progression (Zou et al., 2012). We observed a similar geographic distribution 420

between HBV and HERV-K113 (Figure 5E).  HERV-K directly interacts with exogenous 421

viruses such as HIV to reduce the infectivity of the resulting chimeric virions (Zwolińska 422

et al., 2013). HERV-K-HBV co-option may explain the observed geographic co- 423

occurrence. Alternatively, apolio B RNA editing catalytic component (APOBEC) 424

mediated mutation of HERV-K may increase during HBV infection leading to initial 425

alignment errors and subsequent classification by BLAST (Lee et al., 2008; Vartanian et 426

al., 2010). 427

Discussion 428

In this study, we develop statistical methods for analysis of NIPT data and illustrate the 429

utility of these data for population genetics, association mapping studies, and studies of 430

the human plasma virome.  Despite the low sequencing coverage, we demonstrate that 431

accurate genotype imputation is possible, and we discover novel loci associated with 432

height, BMI and two pregnancy-related traits. The results illustrate the power and 433

feasibility of association mapping using NIPT data. 434

We also leverage the data for population genetic inferences, and show that the 435

majority Han Chinese have evidence of isolation by distance latitudinally, but not 436

longitudinally, presumably due to recent population movements.  In contrast, the genetic 437


<!-- Page 22 -->


22

diversity in ethnic minorities roughly mirrors geography. We successfully identify known 438

and novel loci that are under selection based on the small allele frequency differences in 439

the Han population. Finally, we identify circulating DNA of viruses with clinical 440

relevance in pregnancy (HBV, CMV, ParvoB19) and reveal a different viral sequencing 441

distribution spectrum compared to Europeans. We analyze genetic and viromic data 442

together and reveal a highly significant association between suspected ciHHV-6A/B and 443

MOV10L1-MCL1 hinting at a possible germline variant affecting the integration of 444

HHV-6A/B. 445

Our results illustrate the utility of NIPT data for medical genetic studies, 446

particularly for understanding traits related to fertility and pregnancy.  Furthermore, the 447

availability of large samples of shotgun DNA sequencing from blood opens up new 448

avenues for investigating hypotheses regarding interactions between viruses and host 449

DNA genetic variability. As NIPT testing expands to millions of individuals globally, 450

obtaining informed consent for patients and effective digital curation of medical records 451

should be prioritized by the medical community. 452

Sequencing and QC 924

Details of the sequencing protocol were published previously in (Zhang et al., 2015b). In 925

brief, within 8h of blood collection, plasma was extracted from whole blood after two 926
